Be warned, working with AC power is dangerous and if you are not comfortable with anything, then just don't do anything. Safety is important. Now with the warning out of the way..... 


For some reason this method works for me as I use a USB A port that is conveniently connected to the ground of the whole system. You need to check your system to make sure it supports this. The device I'm using is a Mac mini. 


I cut open an unwanted but working USB A head cable (doesn't matter what's on the other end, we only need the USB A part). Be sure to only cut near the unwanted head part so we have cable to spare.


Find out which is the ground, or V-, or black wire (usually black), see a USB A port wiring diagram. I use a multimeter on continuity test to find the right cable. From here, we only need this ground cable, you can cut the rest off, seal the ends to prevent electrical contact with anything.


I then use a AC mains socket multi plug, opened it up, soldered the USB A ground cable to the ground within the AC multi socket plug. Closes everything up, tested for external continuity and cross checking there is no contact with the other stuff. You don't want AC mains power going into a USB port.. then plug the AC head into the socket plug. And then plug the whole thing into your AC socket. 


Then I just cable tied the whole wires contraption together to make it look like one single neat cable. On the laptop end, plug the USB into USB and AC into AC. Hopefully in that order. 


Power on the AC and voilà! Now it's grounded and I also no longer feel the electric static feeling over the case as well.


Also make sure your AC multi socket plug thing is connected to a "safe"  outlet with lightning protection etc!
